# VOICE — *The Long Book*

A romantasy of the Shelf. 120,000 words, 46 chapters, ~2,600 words each.

---

## 1. The frame

**Person and tense:** third limited, past. Two POVs, alternating by chapter,
never within a chapter. Sahra Ottun carries the odd chapters, Yannu Dral the
even, with two deliberate breaks in the pattern (ch 44–45 both Yannu; ch 46
returns to Sahra) that the reader should feel as a stumble in the rhythm at
exactly the point the rhythm has been broken in the story.

**Chapter headers:** chapter number, POV name, place, tide. *"Nine. Sahra.
Third Reach, low water."* The tide is not decoration — it is the clock the
whole book runs on, and the reader should be able to predict the next
chapter's danger from the header alone by the midpoint.

**No prologue. No epigraphs. No italic dream sequences.** The world is
delivered through people doing work in it.

---

## 2. The register of the world

The Shelf's idiom is **accounting and water**. Its people talk about debt
the way other places talk about weather, and about weather the way other
places talk about God. Two vocabularies run under everything:

- **Ledger words:** entry, carry, rate, assessment, composition, discharge,
  security, distraint, reckoning, struck, credited, owed, short, clear.
- **Water words:** ebb, flood, spring tide, neap, reach, wrack, silt, weep,
  crust, slurry, holding, giving.

These two vocabularies are the book's whole metaphorical economy. A
character reaching outside them for an image is a character who has come
from somewhere else (Yannu, upland-born, thinks in *ground* and *footing*
and *distance*; Sefa Quenn, who predates the trade, thinks in *cloth* and
*handwork* and *hours*), and that difference is the point.

**Diction discipline.** Anglo-Saxon over Latinate. Concrete nouns over
abstract ones. The Le Guin exercise governs description: strong nouns and
verbs, adjectives rationed and adverbs nearly absent. If a sentence can
survive the loss of its adjective, it loses it.

**No modern idiom, ever — including in the romance.** These two do not
banter in twenty-first-century rhythms. Their flirtation is technical: they
argue about rates, correct each other's arithmetic, and give each other
information nobody else is trusted with. When they are being tender they are
being *precise*, which is this world's register of love.

---

## 3. The two narrators

The test is the tag test: strip every attribution and the reader still knows
whose chapter this is by the third sentence.

### Sahra Ottun — the counting voice

Sahra's narration **counts**. She quantifies as a reflex, and the reflex is
her wound: she has been a number in a book since she was nine. Her chapters
carry running totals — carries taken, hours to the flood, years remaining at
the current rate — and the totals intrude on scenes where they have no
business, including the romantic ones.

- Sentence shape: short declaratives, often stacked without conjunction.
  Fragments used as items in a list.
- She narrates her own body as inventory: *nine, and room for five more.*
- She rarely describes a face. She describes hands, cuticles, hairlines —
  the places a load shows — because that is what she was trained to read.
- Interiority arrives as correction: she states a thing, then revises the
  figure. *Four hours. Call it three, with the punt.*
- She does not use the word *want*. She uses *owe*, *need*, *have to*, and
  when she finally uses *want* in ch 23 it should land like a struck match.

**Exemplar (ch 1):**

> Two bays of rot, Ferrey granary, third and fourth. She said it aloud to
> the empty floor, the way her grandmother had said it, the way the Book
> said it, and put her hands flat to the grain.
>
> It came up sweet. It always came up sweet. By the time she had the second
> bay her wrists smelled like a pear left in a coat pocket, and her knees
> had the give in them that meant she was carrying more than she had told
> anyone she could carry. Nine. Room for five. Weyl was four hours late and
> the flood was in two, and she did the arithmetic she did every day, the
> one that came out at sixty-two.
>
> She drank from the cup and it did nothing, and she filled it again.

**Anti-exemplar — what Sahra never sounds like:**

> ~~A wave of exhaustion washed over her. She couldn't help but feel that
> the weight of her family's debt was crushing her spirit. Sahra had always
> been strong, but even she had limits, and today she felt every one of
> them.~~

Three failures: abstract emotion words doing the work of physical detail;
"the weight of" as a metaphor she would never reach for (she would give the
actual number); and a narrator commenting on her own character from outside.

### Yannu Dral — the measuring voice

Yannu's narration **measures distance and reports absence**. He is a
wrack-walker: he has spent six years pacing dead ground and writing down
where it will still take. And he is going grey from the fingertips inward,
so his sensory channel is a channel with a hole in it — the prose must keep
naming what he cannot feel, without pathos, as a matter of fact.

- Sentence shape: longer than Sahra's, but plainer. Subject, verb, object.
  He almost never uses a subordinate clause to hedge.
- He gives distances in paces and times in tides. He does not round, and the
  narration does not round for him. *Two hundred and eleven paces.*
- Negative sensory reporting is his signature: *the shell went under his
  boot and he heard it and did not feel it.*
- He has no interior monologue about his feelings. He has interior monologue
  about *procedure*, and the feelings live in what procedure he chooses.
- He notices what people do with their hands, because hands are the
  currency of his life.

**Exemplar (ch 2):**

> The fourth mark was where he had left it and the ground around it was not.
> He walked it out: two hundred and eleven paces east before the crust rang
> hollow, where last year it had rung at three hundred and forty.
>
> He knelt and put his palm down and got nothing, which told him nothing,
> so he took the glove off and used the back of his hand above the second
> knuckle, where the feeling still reached. Cold. Wet under the white. He
> wrote *129 paces lost, N lobe, silting* in the warrant book and looked at
> the word *silting* for a while, and did not change it.

**Anti-exemplar — what Yannu never sounds like:**

> ~~He gazed out across the endless white expanse of the Whiting, his heart
> heavy with the knowledge of what was coming. Somewhere out there, his
> brother's ghost was waiting. He shivered, though whether from the cold or
> from something deeper, he couldn't say.~~

Three failures: "endless expanse" (he would give a number); a heart doing
metaphorical labour in a man who narrates by procedure; and an ambiguity
about his own sensation, which is the one thing this character is never
vague about — he knows exactly what he can feel and where it stops.

### The seam between them

When the two POVs describe the same object, they should disagree in a way
that is characterological rather than factual. Sahra sees the Wallow as *a
bank that has stopped paying*. Yannu sees it as *ground that has stopped
taking*. Neither is wrong. The reader assembles the third thing.

---

## 4. Magic on the page

The Draw is written as **labour**, not as spectacle. Every working is a job
with a start, a rhythm, a cost, and a mess to clean up afterward.

**Sensations are fixed.** They are set down in `world.md` §Costs and they do
not vary by mood or scene. A drafted chapter that gives salt a new sensation
because the scene wanted a different one is a chapter that has broken the
system. The register does not soften in the intimate scenes: a working done
in a tender chapter costs exactly what a working done in a disaster chapter
costs, and the prose charges it at the same rate.

The five carried loads and their fixed signatures:

| Load | Where it sits | How it is written |
|---|---|---|
| Salt | blood | thirst that water does not touch; whitening at the hairline and in the cuticles; a coin taste at the back of the throat; skin that squeaks under a thumb |
| Rot | joints | sweetness at the wrists you can smell across a table; a give in the knees like wet rope; a slow turning-over sound in the ear |
| Fever | marrow | wet-looking eyes; cold hands and a hot breastbone; a hum in the back teeth |
| Blight | nails and hair | ridged nails that lift at the bed; hair coming out at the temple; cut grass gone over |
| Souring | lungs | a cough with no sickness under it; a taste of standing water |

**Setting** is written from the setter's side as a temperature sequence:
cold from the inside of the hand outward, then hot, then nothing, with a
whine pitched at the jaw. Afterwards, the grey — reported in **spans**, a
fingerbreadth at a time, and always given as a location on the body, never
as a feeling. *To the wrist. To the second knuckle, left.*

**Foundering** has one signature and it is used exactly three times in the
book (ch 9, ch 30, ch 43): **the thirst stops.** That is the whole tell.
No other line describes it. The reader should learn it in ch 9 and be
afraid of it for the remaining three hundred pages.

---

## 5. The romance register

**Heat: open door, twice, and both times brief.** The book is not
closed-door and it is not explicit for its own sake. Its erotic engine is
**touch as a scarce and depreciating resource**: Sahra has not deliberately
touched another person in eleven years, and Yannu can feel less of what he
touches every year of his working life. What would be ordinary contact in
another book is, here, a transaction with a price, and the prose treats it
that way.

Rules for the two scenes:

- **Specific anatomy of numbness.** Where his feeling stops is always
  stated. She works around the border of it; the reader always knows which
  parts of him are receiving and which are not.
- **She narrates aloud.** Because he cannot always tell, Sahra says what she
  is doing while she does it. This is the book's intimacy signature and it
  should be unbearable by ch 42.
- **No swooning vocabulary.** The prose stays as plain in bed as on the
  flats. Restraint is not prudery here; it is the register.
- **The working costs the same.** If magic is used in an intimate scene it
  is billed. There is no tender exemption.

Attraction is never asserted, never explained, and never attributed to
anything but noticing. There is **no bond, tether, mate-mark, or prophecy**
in this world, and none is to be invented in draft to carry a feeling the
scene has not earned.

---

## 6. Dialogue

Attribution is minimal — *said*, and mostly nothing. Action beats over
adverbs. Nobody's eyes widen.

Rules that make the tag test pass:

- **Sahra** answers questions with figures and asks questions only about
  procedure. She does not soften a refusal. Her tic: she repeats a number
  back before she agrees to anything.
- **Yannu** answers what was asked and stops. His tic: he corrects rounding,
  including his own, including when it is rude. He never uses an intensifier
  — no *very*, no *really*, no *so*.
- **Dovra Nesuir** speaks in complete, balanced sentences and never raises
  her voice; she cites instruments by name and clause.
- **Bel Osse** asks questions she already knows the answers to, and her
  metaphors are all about **crowds** and **queues** — she thinks in panic.
- **Halim Nesuir** apologises inside his own sentences, mid-clause.
- **Turi Osse** is obscene, funny, and exact, and uses the second person for
  general truths: *you don't keep your hands, you keep your excuse.*
- **Sefa Quenn** speaks in the old arithmetic — hours and buckets — and her
  sentences are the only ones in the book with proverbs in them.
- **Ansa Rask** speaks in headcounts. Every position she takes is a number
  of people.

---

## 7. Prohibitions

Banned outright, in narration and dialogue both:

*butterflies in her stomach; electricity/sparks between them; the world fell
away; her breath hitched; a heat pooled low in her belly; the bond
thrummed/hummed/sang between them; something ancient and primal; a growl
rumbled through his chest; mine, his magic snarled; power crackled in the
air; he had lived five hundred years and never—; the tether snapped into
place;* and **"the male" / "the female"** as nouns for people.

Also banned, as ordinary craft hygiene:

*a sense of [emotion]; couldn't help but feel; the weight of [abstraction];
the air was thick with; eyes widened; a wave of [emotion] washed over; a
pang of; heart pounded in her chest; hair spilled/cascaded; piercing
[colour] eyes; a knowing smile; ancient wisdom; heavy silence.*

Structural prohibitions:

- **No new capability.** Nothing the Draw can do in the last quarter is
  something it could not visibly do by ch 23.
- **No convenient ground.** The Whiting does not take one more load because
  the scene needs it to.
- **No unpriced touching.** Every set is charged in spans; every carry is
  charged in capacity; the ledger in `braid.md` is the invoice.
- **No overheard half-sentences.** Nothing in this book turns on a
  misunderstanding. Both leads always know exactly where they stand and
  exactly what it costs; the pain is that they are right.

---

## 8. Rhythm and the stability trap

Vary the temperature. The book has quiet chapters on purpose (ch 18, ch 22,
ch 46) and they earn their keep by being where the physical detail thickens.
Alternate long working sequences with short, cold administrative scenes —
the Reckoning House chapters should be the most frightening in the book and
none of them contains a raised voice.

Countermeasures, enforced:

- Things stay broken. Sarrow-under-Wall is not resettled. Turi does not
  survive. The Whiting is not restored — it is *emptied slowly, by people,
  at cost*, and the book ends with that work barely begun.
- Every price in the ledger is permanent. Nothing paid comes back.
- Bel Osse is not converted. She loses the argument and immediately begins
  the next one, and the last thing she says in the book is a threat dressed
  as policy.
- The reader is not told everything. Yannu's falsified warrants land in
  ch 26; the truth about Veth's boots lands in ch 34; the composition's
  acceleration clause is on the page in ch 3 and unremarked until ch 32.
